---
title: "Performance compared with PPforest"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, dpi = 96)
library(ggplot2)

results <- file.path("..", "..", "benchmarks", "results")
speed <- utils::read.csv(file.path(results, "speed.csv"))
memory <- utils::read.csv(file.path(results, "memory.csv"))

# The parameter each experiment varies, and the title of its panel.
varying <- c(
  n = "n", p = "p", p_v05 = "p", q = "q", l = "lambda", v = "pvars", f = "size",
  t_n = "threads", t_p = "threads", t_q = "threads", s_n = "n", s_p = "p", s_q = "q"
)
titles <- c(
  n = "Observations (n)", p = "Variables (p)", p_v05 = "Variables (p), pvars = 0.5",
  q = "Groups (q)", l = "Regularization (lambda)", v = "Variables per split (pvars)",
  f = "Trees (size)", t_n = "Threads, n = 8192", t_p = "Threads, p = 128",
  t_q = "Threads, q = 16", s_n = "Observations (n)", s_p = "Variables (p)", s_q = "Groups (q)"
)

# One row per package and cell, with the varied parameter as `x`.
long <- function(data, experiments) {
  data <- data[data$experiment %in% experiments, ]
  data$x <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(data)), function(i) data[i, varying[[data$experiment[i]]]], numeric(1))
  data$title <- factor(titles[data$experiment], levels = titles[experiments])
  rows <- lapply(c("PPforest", "ppforest2"), function(package) {
    converged <- data[[paste0(package, "_converged")]]
    data.frame(
      title = data$title, x = data$x, package = package, value = data[[package]],
      converged = if (is.null(converged)) TRUE else converged
    )
  })
  rows <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  rows[!is.na(rows$value) & rows$value > 0, ]
}

sweep_plot <- function(data, y) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x, value, colour = package)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(aes(shape = converged), size = 2) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(PPforest = "#E69F00", ppforest2 = "#0072B2")) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    facet_wrap(~title, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = y, colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

# The range of PPforest's value over ppforest2's across an experiment's cells.
ratio_table <- function(data, experiments) {
  rows <- lapply(experiments, function(name) {
    cells <- data[data$experiment == name, ]
    ratio <- cells$PPforest / cells$ppforest2
    values <- cells[[varying[[name]]]]
    data.frame(
      Experiment = titles[[name]],
      Values = paste(format(min(values)), "to", format(max(values))),
      Ratio = sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(ratio), max(ratio))
    )
  })
  knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, rows), row.names = FALSE)
}

thread_axis <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(speed$threads[speed$experiment == "t_n"])))

size_sweeps <- c("n", "p", "p_v05", "q", "l", "v", "f")
thread_sweeps <- c("t_n", "t_p", "t_q")
serial_sweeps <- c("s_n", "s_p", "s_q")
method <- unique(memory$method)
```

ppforest2 is a new implementation of the projection pursuit forests of
`PPforest`. Vidal
(2026) compares the two implementations' training time and memory over the
size of the problem, the hyperparameters and the number of threads
(<https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12008/56830>). This article reproduces those
experiments at a smaller scale, with the scripts in
[`benchmarks/`](https://github.com/andres-vidal/ppforest2-r/tree/main/benchmarks).
The grids start where the two implementations begin to differ and stop at
sizes that run on a laptop, and forests have fewer trees than in the thesis, so
the figures reproduce the shape of each result but not its magnitudes.

Each experiment varies one parameter on data simulated with the thesis's
generator: `q` groups of normal observations in `p` variables, with random
means and covariances. Both packages train forests of the same size, with the
same `lambda` and the same number of variables per split. Each measurement is
repeated until it is stable (see `benchmarks/README.md`).

The results below were computed on this machine:

```{r environment, comment = ""}
writeLines(readLines(file.path(results, "speed-environment.txt")))
```

## Training time

### Size of the problem

With all the cores of the machine, ppforest2 trains faster in every
experiment. The gap widens with the number of observations, and stays in a
narrower band over the number of variables, the number of groups and the
hyperparameters. Open points mark cells whose times did not stabilize: the
fastest ppforest2 fits take a few milliseconds, which `system.time()` measures
coarsely.

```{r speed-size, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Training time of PPforest and ppforest2 against each varied parameter, on a log scale."}
sweep_plot(long(speed, size_sweeps), "Training time (s)")
```

```{r speed-size-ratio}
ratio_table(speed, size_sweeps)
```

The ratio is the time of `PPforest` over that of ppforest2.

### One thread

With one thread, the comparison isolates the algorithms from how each package
runs in parallel. The gap still widens with the number of observations.

```{r speed-serial, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Training time of PPforest and ppforest2 with one thread against the number of observations, variables and groups, on a log scale."}
sweep_plot(long(speed, serial_sweeps), "Training time (s)")
```

```{r speed-serial-ratio}
ratio_table(speed, serial_sweeps)
```

### Threads

The speedup is the time with one thread over the time with `t` threads; the
dashed line is a perfect speedup. ppforest2 trains its trees in threads of one
process and speeds up in all three settings. PPforest forks worker processes,
and gains little when the observations dominate the problem, because most of
its time is spent in the parent process.

```{r speed-threads, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Speedup of PPforest and ppforest2 against the number of threads, with a dashed line for a perfect speedup."}
speedup <- speed[speed$experiment %in% thread_sweeps, ]
speedup <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(speedup, speedup$experiment), function(cells) {
  cells$PPforest <- cells$PPforest[cells$threads == 1] / cells$PPforest
  cells$ppforest2 <- cells$ppforest2[cells$threads == 1] / cells$ppforest2
  cells
}))
sweep_plot(long(speedup, thread_sweeps), "Speedup") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  thread_axis
```

## Memory

Memory is the peak the training adds to an R session: the peak of a process
that trains a forest, minus that of one that only loads the packages and
simulates the same data. These results were measured with **`r method`**.

```{r memory-method, results = "asis"}
if (identical(method, "sampled RSS, one process")) {
  cat(
    "On macOS, the memory a forked worker shares with its parent cannot be",
    "told apart from its own, so only single processes are measured: the size",
    "sweeps run with one thread for both packages, and the thread sweeps",
    "measure ppforest2 alone. On Linux the scripts measure every process,",
    "including the worker processes of `PPforest`.\n"
  )
}
```

### Size of the problem

ppforest2 adds less memory in every experiment. The gap is widest over the
number of observations, where the memory of `PPforest` grows faster than
linearly, and narrowest over the number of variables, where both
implementations store dense matrices of the size of `p` squared. Over the
number of groups, the memory of ppforest2 grows faster than that of
`PPforest`, so the ratio narrows, as in the thesis. The smallest ppforest2
figures are a few megabytes over a baseline of about a hundred, so their
ratios are approximate.

```{r memory-size, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Peak memory added by training in PPforest and ppforest2 against each varied parameter, on a log scale."}
sweep_plot(long(memory, size_sweeps), "Peak memory added (MB)")
```

```{r memory-size-ratio}
ratio_table(memory, size_sweeps)
```

The ratio is the memory of `PPforest` over that of ppforest2.

### Threads

Each ppforest2 thread keeps its own working memory, so the peak grows
modestly with the number of threads.

```{r memory-threads, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Peak memory added by training in ppforest2 against the number of threads."}
sweep_plot(long(memory, thread_sweeps), "Peak memory added (MB)") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  thread_axis
```

## Reproducing the results

The scripts run from the repository root with both packages installed. See
[`benchmarks/README.md`](https://github.com/andres-vidal/ppforest2-r/blob/main/benchmarks/README.md)
for the versions and for running a subset of the experiments.

```sh
Rscript benchmarks/speed.R
Rscript benchmarks/memory.R
```
